mappings.note: Hands-on: strip the seed coat and compare chickpea with maize. The student performs the investigation (LO-4) and the finding is the dicot/monocot contrast (LO-2). Not LO-3, because two named seeds are contrasted rather than a set being sorted.

Groups compare the BASIS each chose for grouping plants. LO-3 for classifying on observable properties; LO-13 because the point of the item is accepting that another group's basis is equally valid, which is objectivity and freedom from prejudice.
Differences in roots and leaf venation between two seed types. Taproot versus fibrous root is LO-2's own worked example; LO-3 would be wrong because nothing is sorted into named classes.
Sorts ten named animals into aquatic, terrestrial and both. A classification of organisms by an observable property, which is exactly LO-3.
Radish: name the root type and predict the venation. Runs the taproot/fibrous distinction in both directions, LO-2. Not LO-10, since the kitchen garden is only the setting, not the thing assessed.

Mountain goat versus plains goat: the differences are LO-2, and 'what are the reasons for these differences' demands the habitat adaptation, which is LO-5's own example of relating adaptation to habitat.
Same stem as the preceding item (its answer table has been concatenated into the stem). Mapped identically: structural differences LO-2, cause of those differences LO-5.
Students collect and observe plant roots, then replant them. The observation is the investigation (LO-4) and the deliverable is the root difference between figures (a) and (b) (LO-2).
Asks whether many more varieties exist beyond those on the board -- the scale of biodiversity. No LO in this frame covers biodiversity as such, so cited at the goal that carries 'concern for life'.

Stem is a stray table row ('Earthworm Crawls Body segments, muscles, setae'), but the answer groups ant, goat, pigeon, housefly, fish and snake by the body parts they move with. Grouping organisms on an observable property is LO-3.

Stem is a stray list of five organism names, but the answer contrasts desert and other regions and explains camel, cactus and scorpion features as adaptations to heat and scarce water -- LO-5, relating organisms to their habitat.

Stem is a stray table row for the lemon plant, but the answer sorts mango, rose and others into tree, shrub and herb by stem hardness, thickness and branching height. Herbs/shrubs/trees is LO-3's own example set.

Group nine animals on a feature the chapter did NOT discuss. LO-3 for the classification, and LO-12 because inventing an unused basis is creativity in planning, which is what the 'other than those discussed' clause marks.
Deforestation for a growing population: effect on surroundings and how to address it. The 'how to address' half makes this the protect-the-environment outcome rather than LO-5's causal relating.

Reads a flow-chart and supplies examples for branches A and B, which turn out to be reticulate and parallel venation. LO-8 for working with the flow chart, LO-2 for the venation distinction it encodes.
Sanjay must frame clarifying questions about a shrub claim. CG-SCI2 because the deliverable is questions, not an answer; LO-3 because what is in dispute is the herb/shrub/tree classification.
Dicot-taproot versus monocot-fibrous table, with the further similarities of each group. The differentiation LO, whose stated example is tap versus fibrous roots.

Duck's webbed feet versus other birds, and what the duck can do with them. Structure tied to the way of life -- adaptation, LO-5. Not LO-1: the item is not satisfied by naming the feature, it wants the function it enables.
Definition of biodiversity. The 13-outcome frame has no biodiversity outcome; CG-SCI4 carries 'concern for life' and is the honest level for it.
Observe the nature walk without disturbing living creatures. Respect for life, the CG-SCI4 goal text. Not LO-13, whose values are honesty, objectivity and cooperation between people.
Why grouping organisms matters -- the rationale for classification itself, LO-3.
Soft green tender stems are herbs. LO-3 lists 'plants as herbs, shrubs, trees, creepers and climbers' as its own example.
Rose as an example of a shrub -- placing a named plant into the LO-3 category set.
The basis of the herb/shrub/tree split is height and stem nature. This names the classification criterion, the core of LO-3.
Definition of venation as the pattern of veins. Identifying an organism by an observable feature, LO-1; no comparison is made, so LO-2 would overstate it.
Reticulate versus parallel venation, net-like against side-by-side. A structural differentiation between two types, LO-2.
Names the root system that has one main root with side roots. Recognising a structure from its described features, LO-1; the contrast with fibrous roots is not asked for.
Grass has fibrous roots. This requires holding the tap/fibrous contrast, LO-2's named example, and assigning grass to the right side of it.
The general reticulate-taproot and parallel-fibrous correlation. Both distinctions of LO-2 at once; not LO-5, because this is a structural association, not a cause.
What cotyledons are -- identifying a seed part from its observable behaviour (a chickpea splits). LO-1.
Maize has one cotyledon. The cotyledon count is the monocot/dicot discriminator, so this is LO-2 rather than plain identification.
Dicots have reticulate venation and taproots. Holds the full dicot/monocot contrast on two structures at once, LO-2.
Which is NOT a basis for classifying animals (the sounds they make). Tests what counts as a valid classification criterion, LO-3.
A fish swimming with fins belongs to the movement-and-body-parts category. Assigning an observation to a classification axis, LO-3.
Definition of adaptation as features that allow survival in a particular habitat. LO-5 names 'adaptations of animals and plants with their habitats' as its own example.
Forests as a terrestrial habitat. Sorting habitats into named classes, LO-3; not LO-5, as no adaptation is involved.
Why hot-desert biodiversity differs from cold-mountain biodiversity: different adaptations for different conditions. A cause asked for explicitly, LO-5.
Definition of habitat as the place where organisms live. Cited at LO-3 because habitat is the frame this chapter sorts organisms by; LO-5 is reserved for items that actually ask about adaptation.
The deodar's conical shape lets snow slide off. A structure explained by the demand of its habitat -- LO-5.

How habitat damage causes biodiversity loss. LO-5 for the causal chain the item asks for, CG-SCI4 for the conservation register. Not LO-11, which requires the student to make protective efforts, not merely explain the harm.
The Chipko movement. LO-11 explicitly covers spreading awareness and efforts to protect the environment, which is what the movement is.
Sacred groves as forest patches communities protect. Community protection of the environment, LO-11.
Salim Ali as the Birdman of India. A biographical fact about a naturalist; no LO covers scientists' lives, so cited at the goal carrying concern for life.
Animals spreading seeds after eating fruit as interdependence. Explaining an ecological process, LO-6; not LO-5, since the item asks what illustrates interdependence rather than what causes it.
Which is NOT a tree characteristic (soft green stems). Tests the boundary between the tree and herb classes, LO-3.
How climbers and creepers differ in growth habit. Although both are LO-3 categories, the verb here is 'differ' on the basis of structure and support, so LO-2 is the closer outcome.
Predicts a taproot from net-like venation. Applies the venation/root differentiation to an unseen plant, LO-2.
Assertion-reason on camels' concentrated urine as water conservation in arid habitats. The reason clause IS the adaptation-to-habitat link, LO-5.

Evaluates statements about habitat damage and biodiversity. The stem carries only one of the three statements its options reference, so the item is cited at goal level for concern for life rather than to a specific LO.
A medium plant with woody stems branching near the ground is a shrub. Applies the LO-3 category set to a fresh field observation.
Janaki Ammal and the Botanical Survey of India's documentation of plant diversity. A biography item; no LO reaches it, so the goal carrying concern for life.
Why frogs differ from fish and goats: they occupy both water and land. Sorting by habitat class, LO-3.
Two-cotyledon plants are dicots. Names a class from a property, so classification (LO-3) rather than the dicot/monocot contrast itself.
Project Tiger's launch year. A conservation programme, so LO-11; the date alone is recall but the subject is environmental protection.
Distinguishes a tree stem from a herb stem on hardness, thickness and colour. A property-based differentiation, LO-2.
Which feature does NOT vary among plants (photosynthesis). Tests which observable features -- height, leaf shape, flower colour and scent -- are available for identification, LO-1.
Predicts fibrous roots from parallel venation, the monocot direction of the same correlation. LO-2.
Assertion-reason: regional biodiversity varies because organisms carry adaptations to local conditions. The reason is the adaptation-habitat link, LO-5.
The term for animals living in water and on land. Naming a habitat-based class, LO-3.
Chickpea has a taproot and reticulate venation like sadabahar. Requires both halves of the dicot/monocot differentiation, LO-2.
